blocks.text: The **rotator cuff** is a group of four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis) whose tendons surround the shoulder joint. They keep the ball centred in the socket and help lift and rotate the arm.

**Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain (RCRSP)** is the modern umbrella term for pain on the outer shoulder, often worse with lifting the arm or lying on it, where the cuff tendons are the likely main source [Ref - to verify]. It replaces older labels such as subacromial impingement syndrome because we cannot reliably prove that a tendon is being pinched, and the old labels suggested a mechanism that is not well supported. RCRSP includes cuff tendinopathy, partial-thickness tears and some full-thickness tears.
Tendon changes on scans are very common in people without pain, and become more common with age [Ref - to verify]. A scan finding does not always explain the pain.

items: Gradual pain on the outer or upper arm, often with overhead activity, reaching behind, and lying on the side at night.
Painful arc during raising or lowering the arm, usually in the middle range.
Weakness may appear because of pain, or because of a larger tear.
No clear stiffness of passive movement, unlike frozen shoulder.
**Acute tear picture:** sudden pain and weakness after a fall or heavy lift, especially in a younger person or in someone who cannot lift the arm. This needs early medical opinion (see G).

rows: Where is the pain, and does it spread below the elbow?
Outer arm pain fits cuff; pain below elbow with neck link suggests the neck
What movements and positions hurt? Overhead, behind the back, lying on that side?
Was there a fall, pull or sudden pop?
Any sudden weakness or inability to lift the arm?
Any neck pain, numbness or pins and needles?
Any night pain that is constant and not position-related?
Any recent increase in lifting, throwing, swimming or work load?
Diabetes, thyroid disease, smoking, steroid use?
Chest pain, breathlessness, sweating with left shoulder pain?
What do you most want to do again?

items: Observe posture, muscle wasting (supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae), scapular position.
Cervical screen (active movements, Spurling if indicated) to exclude a neck source.
Active shoulder movement: elevation, rotation, hand behind back; note painful arc and scapular movement.
Passive range: compare with the other side. Large loss suggests a different diagnosis (frozen shoulder, arthritis).
Resisted tests of each cuff muscle (below).
Special tests (Section E).
Palpation of the tendon insertions, biceps tendon, AC joint.
Neurological screen of the upper limb.

blocks.text: Honest note: no single test is perfect. Painful tests suggest the cuff region is irritable, but they do not identify exactly which tendon or whether there is a tear. Combine tests [Ref - to verify].
E1. Painful arc

rows: Look for pain in the mid-range of arm elevation, a common feature of RCRSP
Ask the patient to raise the arm out to the side (abduction) and lower it slowly; ask where the pain starts and stops
Pain in a mid-range arc (often reported between about 60 and 120 degrees), easing at the top or bottom [Ref - to verify]
A positive result supports a cuff-related source
Also positive in other shoulder conditions

blocks.text: E2. Hawkins-Kennedy test

rows: Provoke pain by moving the greater tuberosity toward the area beneath the acromion
Beside the patient; one hand on the elbow and one on the wrist
Raise the arm to 90 degrees of forward flexion with the elbow bent to 90 degrees, then passively rotate the forearm downward (internal rotation)
Reproduction of the patient's familiar shoulder pain
Supports a cuff-related pain source when combined with other tests
Low specificity; many shoulder problems cause pain here [Ref - to verify]
Moving too fast; allowing trunk rotation; counting a stretch feeling as positive
Resisted tests for strength and pain

blocks.text: E3. Resisted external rotation (infraspinatus) and full/empty can (supraspinatus)

rows: Elbow at the side, bent to 90 degrees. Patient pushes the hand outward against the therapist's resistance. Positive: pain or weakness
Arm raised in the scapular plane (about 30 degrees forward of the side), thumb pointing up. Patient resists downward pressure. Positive: pain or weakness
As above but thumb pointing down. More likely to provoke pain; full can is often preferred [Ref - to verify]
Pain with good strength suggests tendinopathy. Marked weakness suggests a larger tear or a nerve problem

blocks.text: E4. Combined cluster

A published cluster uses painful arc, weakness in external rotation (infraspinatus test) and a positive Hawkins-Kennedy test. If all three are present, the likelihood of a cuff-related problem increases [Ref - to verify exact criteria]. A cluster does not prove a tear.
E5. Tests for a full-thickness tear

rows: Therapist passively lifts the arm to 90 degrees abduction. Patient slowly lowers it
Arm drops or cannot be lowered smoothly, or severe pain
Arm held in about 20 degrees of elevation and near full external rotation. Therapist releases the wrist
The arm cannot hold the position and drifts inward
Suggests a larger supraspinatus or infraspinatus tear
Hand behind the back, lift the hand away from the back (lift-off); or press the abdomen with the elbow forward (belly press)
Cannot lift the hand away, or the elbow drops back

blocks.text: These tests have better specificity than sensitivity in many reports [Ref - to verify], so a positive result is more informative than a negative one. If a large tear is suspected, refer for imaging and medical review.

rows: Marked loss of passive range, especially external rotation
Stiffness, grinding, older age, loss of passive external rotation
Neck-related arm pain, neurological signs, Spurling positive
Pain on top of the shoulder, cross-body adduction pain, local tenderness
Anterior shoulder pain, tenderness over the long head
Nerve problem (suprascapular, long thoracic, neuralgic amyotrophy)
Wasting, scapular winging, severe pain then weakness
Not changed by shoulder movement, systemic features

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness with left shoulder or arm pain
Fall or injury with deformity, inability to move the arm, or severe pain
Support the arm; refer for imaging
Sudden inability to lift the arm after injury or lift, especially under 60 years
**Urgent medical review** (early repair may be considered) [Ref - to verify]
Weight loss, cancer history, constant night pain, hard mass
Shoulder and arm pain with Horner signs (droopy eyelid, small pupil), hand muscle wasting, smoker
Arm swelling, pain and colour change
Bilateral shoulder stiffness and aching with morning stiffness, older age, fatigue
Refer; ask about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Neck source? Cervical screen positive: go to Vol 2.
Large loss of passive range? **Yes:** frozen shoulder or arthritis pathway.
Lateral shoulder pain, mid-range painful arc, resisted pain with normal passive range? **Yes:** working diagnosis is rotator cuff-related shoulder pain.
Drop arm, lag sign or marked weakness, or recent trauma? **Yes:** suspect a larger tear; refer for imaging.
Otherwise: start exercise-based care.

rows: May ease shoulder movement and short-term pain [Ref - to verify]
Stiff thoracic spine with raised-arm pain
Prone or sitting, gentle central or unilateral glides
Supine, gentle oscillations in a pain-free range

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education plus an exercise program. Manual therapy is optional for short-term symptom relief. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs a tendon, frees a trapped tendon or fixes scapular position. Evidence supports exercise as the main component [Ref - to verify].
**Is it working?** Look for easier arm elevation, a smaller painful arc and better overhead or lifting function.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** exercise loads the tendon at a level the patient tolerates and then increases gradually. Pain during exercise of up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is commonly used as a guide [Ref - to verify]. Do not choose exercises to fix position alone.

rows: Pain relief and early cuff loading
Standing sideways, elbow at 90 degrees, push the back of the hand into a wall; hold
5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice daily [Ref - to verify]
Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasts into next day
Stand beside a wall, arm slightly out, push the elbow into the wall
Elbow at the side with a rolled towel, rotate out against a light band
Side-lying external rotation or prone row
Arm raised in the scapular plane with a light weight
Serratus wall slide or push-up plus
Hands on wall, slide up and press
Gradual overhead press, carry, throwing progression

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** discomfort that settles quickly is acceptable. Pain that stays high into the next day means reduce load. New weakness, numbness or night pain means reassess.

rows: Weak or no added benefit [Ref - to verify]
Possible option mainly in calcific tendinopathy
Short-term cue or comfort; no proven healing effect

blocks.text: **Medical options:** corticosteroid injection may reduce pain in the short term but may not improve long-term outcomes and has been associated with tendon risks in some studies [Ref - to verify]. Decisions about injections and surgery belong to the doctor. Trials of subacromial decompression surgery have not shown clear benefit over placebo surgery or exercise for many people [Ref - to verify].

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags and the neck, explain what RCRSP is and that it usually improves with loading, reassure about scan findings, advise on load.
**Early:** relative rest from the worst aggravators (not complete rest), isometrics, gentle movement.
**Middle:** progressive strengthening of cuff and scapular muscles; thoracic mobility.
**Late:** overhead, lifting, sport-specific or work-specific loading; plan for maintenance.
**If no improvement:** review diagnosis and adherence; consider medical or surgical opinion. Many trials use around 12 weeks of exercise before reviewing [Ref - to verify], but each patient differs.

blocks.text: Record pain scale, painful arc, active range, strength against resistance, a shoulder questionnaire (for example the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index or QuickDASH) [Ref - to verify], and goal tasks.

rows: Pain and function improve, strength increases
No change after about 6 to 12 weeks of well-delivered exercise
Review diagnosis; consider imaging and medical opinion
New weakness, loss of range, night pain

blocks.text: **Case:** A 52-year-old electrician has 3 months of right outer shoulder pain, worse overhead and when lying on that side. Passive range is full and painless apart from end range. Painful arc is positive. External rotation strength is pain-limited but strong. Hawkins-Kennedy is positive. Drop arm is negative. No red flags and a normal neck examination.

**Working diagnosis:** right rotator cuff-related shoulder pain. **Plan:** education, isometric external rotation and abduction for pain, progression to banded rotation and scaption, thoracic mobility, work-load advice, reassess every 2 to 3 weeks.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why do we avoid saying the tendon is pinched? Evidence for a pinching mechanism is limited, and the idea may create fear of movement. A load-based explanation is more consistent with the evidence [Ref - to verify].
Why check the neck in a patient with shoulder pain? Neck problems can refer pain to the shoulder, and treating the shoulder alone would not help.
Passive range is greatly reduced in all directions. Which chapter applies? Adhesive capsulitis (Ch 2) or glenohumeral arthritis, not RCRSP.
A 35-year-old cannot lift his arm after a fall. What next? Suspect an acute tear or other injury, protect the shoulder and refer for urgent medical assessment.
Why use isometric exercises first? They can reduce pain without much tendon movement and allow loading when the shoulder is irritable [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** education and graded exercise.
**Justifying findings:** lateral shoulder pain, painful arc, resisted pain, full passive range, no flags.
**Priority:** tendon loading and function.
**Manual therapy:** optional adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, then banded rotation, scaption, scapular control and functional loading.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** common, usually improves, scan changes are normal with age, movement is safe.
**Avoid:** complete rest, fear-based explanations, heavy overhead load during a flare.
**Measure:** pain, painful arc, strength, SPADI or QuickDASH, goal task.
**If no improvement:** review diagnosis and refer for medical opinion.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** goals met, strength and function restored, home program in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, atraumatic, no red flags, full passive range.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise improves pain and function; how test clusters relate to imaging findings.
**Hypotheses:** that tendon loading changes tendon capacity; that scapular exercises work through scapular position (uncertain).
**Future questions:** best loading dose and which patients benefit from injection or surgery.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain RCRSP in plain language.
Perform painful arc, Hawkins-Kennedy and resisted cuff tests and state their limits.
Recognise signs of a larger tear and know when to refer.
Build a starting exercise plan.
